title: Central Ideas and Details, Part 1: The Method and Two Questions

beats.say: Central ideas and details questions ask what a short text is mostly about, or what it says about one specific point.

card.text: What is the text mostly about?

beats.say: There are two kinds. A main idea question asks which choice best states the main idea of the text. A detail question asks what the text says about one thing.
The passages can be informational, such as science, history, or the arts, or literary, which is a short excerpt from a story.
Step one. Read the question first, so you know whether it asks for the main idea or for a detail.
Step two. Read the text once, and notice any turn word, such as however, but, or yet. The turn usually leads to the real point.
Step three. For a main idea, say a ten-word summary in your head before you read the choices. For a detail, find the exact line.
Step four. Eliminate choices that are too narrow, too broad, or unsupported. Between two survivors, pick the one you can prove line by line.

scenes.title: Four kinds of wrong answer
rows: Does it cover the whole text?
Does the text go that far?
Can you point to the line?

beats.say: A too narrow answer is true, but it only covers one sentence. Test it by asking whether it covers the whole text.
A too broad answer makes claims about all or most things, or about a bigger topic. Test it by asking whether the text really goes that far.
A distorted answer uses the words of the text, but changes the relationship between the ideas, such as the cause or the comparison.
An off-topic answer sounds reasonable, but the text never mentions it. Test it by asking whether you can point to the line.
Easy question. We will read a short informational text, and then answer a main idea question. Remember to look for a turn word, and to summarize before reading the choices.

scenes.title: Read the text
scenes.text: Many gardeners believe that watering plants every day keeps them healthy. However, researchers at one agricultural college found that tomato plants watered deeply twice a week grew stronger roots than plants watered daily. The deeper roots helped the plants survive dry weeks.

beats.say: The text begins with a common belief, that daily watering keeps plants healthy. Notice that this is a view that the author is about to correct.
The word however is the turn. The real point comes after it: deep watering twice a week grew stronger roots than daily watering.
The last sentence adds support. The deeper roots helped the plants survive dry weeks. Our ten-word summary is, deep watering twice weekly beats daily watering for tomatoes.

scenes.title: Which choice best states the main idea?
scenes.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

options.A: Gardeners should stop watering tomato plants entirely.
options.B: Deep, less frequent watering can produce stronger tomato plants than daily watering.
options.C: Tomato plants grow best in dry weather.
options.D: Agricultural colleges teach gardeners how to grow tomatoes.

beats.say: Compare each choice with our summary. Choice A says gardeners should stop watering entirely. The text only compares two watering schedules, so this is too extreme.
Choice C says tomatoes grow best in dry weather. The text only says deeper roots helped plants survive dry weeks, so this distorts the relationship.
Choice D is about what agricultural colleges teach. The text never says that, so it is off-topic.
Choice B matches our summary, and it matches the contrast set up by however. The answer is B.
Medium question. This time the question asks for a detail. For a detail, the answer must be directly stated in the text, or be a very close paraphrase. If you have to guess, it is wrong.

scenes.title: Read the text
scenes.text: When the lights went out during the storm, Priya did not panic. She found a flashlight in the kitchen drawer, then walked down the hall to check on her younger brother, who was asleep. Only after she had made sure he was safe did she begin to look for candles.

beats.say: The question will ask what Priya did, so we read for her actions in order. First she stays calm, and finds a flashlight.
Next she checks on her younger brother, and only after that does she look for candles. The words only after tell us the order.

scenes.title: According to the text: Priya
scenes.question: According to the text, what did Priya do after the lights went out?

options.A: She woke her brother and led him outside.
options.B: She checked on her brother before looking for candles.
options.C: She panicked and called her parents.
options.D: She finished her homework by candlelight.

beats.say: Choice A says she woke her brother and led him outside. The text says he was asleep, and never says she took him outside, so this is not stated.
Choice C contradicts the text, because the text says she did not panic.
Choice D mentions homework, which the text never mentions, so it is off-topic.
Choice B is directly stated. She checked on her brother, and only after that did she begin to look for candles. The answer is B.
To recap. Read the question first, notice the turn word, and summarize the text in about ten words before reading the choices.
Eliminate answers that are too narrow, too broad, distorted, or off-topic. For a detail, the answer must be directly stated.
beats.item: Eliminate by type; details are stated
